paragraphs.text: Rosh Hashanah 3a — “Rav Chisda said: They taught this only concerning the kings of Israel, but for the kings of the nations of the world we count from Tishrei, as it is said, ‘The words of Nechemyah son of Chachalyah: It happened in the month of Kislev, in the twentieth year ...’; and it is written, ‘It happened in the month of Nisan, in the twentieth year of Artachshasta ...’.” The two events retain the same regnal year across Nisan. The distinction between the two systems is the starting point of Rav Tzadok’s account of solar and lunar kingship.

paragraphs.text: Shemot Rabbah 15:27 — “The Holy One, blessed be He, entrusted the secret of the moon to Israel so that they would count by it, while the nations count by the sun. This teaches: Just as the sun is only by day, so they rule only in this world; and just as the sun is of fire, so they will be judged through it. ... Just as the moon is visible by day and by night, so Israel rules in this world and in the world to come. Just as the moon is of light, so Israel inherits light, as it is said: ‘Light is sown for the righteous, and gladness for the upright of heart.’” The Midrash’s contrast is a symbolic exposition of inheritance and judgment. Rav Tzadok develops the distinction between receiving the sun’s illumination and encountering its consuming fire.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Likkutei Maamarim, Yehoshua 1 — “Therefore Yisrael reckon by the moon and the nations by the sun, for the nations imagine they eat and drink of their own, self-sufficient and lacking nothing.” Rav Tzadok there gives the inner meaning of counting by the moon. Yisrael know nothing is their own and only receive. The nations’ “fire” is a claim to self-sufficiency.

paragraphs.text: Nedarim 8b — “Reish Lakish said: There is no Gehinnom in the world to come. Rather, the Holy One, blessed be He, brings the sun out of its sheath: the righteous are healed through it, and the wicked are judged through it, as it is said, ‘For you who fear My name, a sun ... shall rise.’ Not only that: they take delight in it, as it is said, ‘You will go out and leap like calves of the stall.’ The wicked are judged through it, as it is said, ‘Behold, the day comes, burning like an oven.’” The same revelation brings healing or judgment. Rav Tzadok explains the righteous person’s reception through the image of the moon receiving light.

paragraphs.text: Shemot Rabbah 15:26 — “The moon begins to shine on the first of Nisan. As it proceeds, it grows brighter until fifteen days, and its disk becomes full. From the fifteenth until the thirtieth its light diminishes; on the thirtieth it is not seen. So Israel has fifteen generations from Avraham until Shlomo. Avraham began to shine ... Yitzchak came and he too shone ... Yaakov came and added light. ... When Shlomo came, the disk of the moon became full, as it is said: ‘Shlomo sat upon Hashem’s throne as king.’” The Midrash lists the intervening generations and then the corresponding decline. Rav Tzadok focuses on Avraham as the beginning and Shlomo as the fullness of the royal illumination.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Chayei Sarah 5 — “All of Avraham Avinu’s words of Torah were at the level of Torah she'b'al peh alone, for he kept even the rabbinic mitzvos; all the Torah he learned was from his heart.” The Gemara cited there is Yoma 28b. This shows why Avraham is the beginning of the Oral Torah’s light. He had no Written Torah to receive from, and his own heart was the source.

paragraphs.text: Bereshit Rabbah 42:5 — “‘The valley of Shaveh’—Rabbi Berechyah and Rabbi Chelbo said in Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachman’s name: There all the nations agreed, cut cedar trees, made him a great platform, and seated him above it. They praised him and said: ‘Hear us, my lord; you are a prince of God among us.’ They said: ‘You are king over us, prince over us, a god over us.’ He replied: ‘Let the world not lack its King, and let the world not lack its God.’” The offer of rule is explicitly answered by Avraham’s refusal to displace divine sovereignty. That qualification is central to Rav Tzadok’s ensuing distinction between human elevation and God’s kingship.

paragraphs.text: Zohar III 210b, Balak — “‘For from the head of rocks I see him.’ Rabbi Yitzchak said: ‘From the head of rocks’—these are the patriarchs, as it is written, ‘Look to the rock from which you were hewn.’ ‘From the hills I behold him’—these are the mothers. From this side and from that side they cannot be cursed.” The 210b marker precedes this paragraph and 211a follows. Although the singular “rock” in Yeshayahu’s context points to Avraham, the Zohar applies the plural rocks to all the patriarchs, precisely the extension that Rav Tzadok discusses.

paragraphs.text: Zohar III 150a, Behaaloscha — “‘A well that princes dug, that the generous ones of the people excavated.’ The well is the congregation of Israel. ‘Princes dug it’—this is Father and Mother, who gave birth to her. ‘The generous ones of the people excavated it’—these are the patriarchs, as it is written, ‘The generous ones of the peoples gathered, the people of the God of Avraham.’” The quoted words precede the embedded 150b marker and belong to III 150a. The use of “patriarchs” despite the proof-verse naming Avraham is the point Rav Tzadok develops.

paragraphs.text: Chagigah 3a — “Rava expounded: What is meant by ‘How beautiful are your steps in sandals, daughter of the generous one’? How beautiful are Israel’s feet when they go up for the festival pilgrimage. ‘Daughter of the generous one’—the daughter of Avraham our father, who is called generous, as it is said, ‘The generous ones of the peoples gathered, the people of the God of Avraham.’ ‘The God of Avraham,’ and not the God of Yitzchak and Yaakov? Rather, the God of Avraham, who was the first of the converts.” The Gemara explains why this verse names Avraham particularly. Rav Tzadok compares this particular naming with the Zohar’s inclusive application to the patriarchs.

paragraphs.text: Bava Metzia 83a — “His father said to him: ‘My son, even if you make for them a banquet like Shlomo’s in his time, you have not fulfilled your obligation to them, for they are the children of Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov. Rather, before they begin work, go and tell them: On condition that you have a claim against me only for bread and legumes.’ Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel said: He did not need to say this; everything follows the local custom.” The Mishnah concerns a promise of food made to hired laborers without qualification. The mention of all three patriarchs is what Rav Tzadok compares with the Gemara’s example drawn specifically from Avraham’s hospitality.

paragraphs.text: Bava Metzia 86b — “Does this mean that Avraham our father’s banquet was superior to Shlomo’s? ... Yet concerning Avraham it is written: ‘Avraham ran to the herd and took a calf, tender and good’; Rav Yehudah said in Rav’s name: ‘A calf’—one; ‘tender’—two; ‘good’—three.” The Gemara develops the comparison through the quantities and recipients of the meals. Rav Tzadok’s point is that a proof drawn from Avraham can express the dignity of the descendants of all three patriarchs. The cited Gemara’s banquet comparison is distinct from the Mishnah’s general mention of all three patriarchs.

paragraphs.text: Tikkunei Zohar 77b — “Concerning these two lights it is said: two faces, male and female. ‘Let there be light’—this is Pesach, ‘on the evening of the fourteenth.’ ‘There was light’—this is Rosh Hashanah, of which it is said, ‘It happened on the day’: here ‘it happened’ and there ‘it happened,’ and in every place ‘it happened’ is an expression of distress.” The original text explicitly juxtaposes Pesach and Rosh Hashanah through the two light phrases. Rav Tzadok explains the first as the beginning of the Oral Torah’s renewal and the second as its illumination through reception from the Written Torah.

paragraphs.text: Vayikra Rabbah 2:4 — “Rabbi Avin said: This is like a king who had purple garments. He would instruct his servant: ‘Attend to this one; fold it and shake it.’ The servant said: ‘My lord king, of all your purple garments, you instruct me only concerning this one?’ He replied: ‘This is the one I wore on the day of my kingship.’ So Moshe said before the Holy One, blessed be He: ‘Master of the world, of the seventy nations in Your world, You instruct me only concerning Israel?’ He replied: ‘They first proclaimed Me king at the sea and said to Me, ‘Hashem shall reign forever and ever.’’” Israel’s special place is explained through its first proclamation of God’s kingship. The following parable in the Midrash separately speaks of Israel’s acceptance at Sinai.

paragraphs.text: Deuteronomy 17:15 — “You shall surely set over yourself a king whom Hashem your God chooses. From among your brothers shall you set a king over yourself; you may not place over yourself a foreign man who is not your brother.” The Torah establishes the appointment and its restrictions. Rav Tzadok’s wording here explains the authorized place of an earthly king within his distinction between present and future divine kingship.

paragraphs.text: Isaiah 33:22 — “For Hashem is our judge, Hashem is our lawgiver, Hashem is our king; He will save us.” The three titles ground Rav Tzadok’s distinction between the Written Torah, the Oral Torah’s judges, and royal judgment, whose ultimate unification reveals divine salvation.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Derashos HaRan, discourse 11:3–4 — “The Holy One assigned each of these matters to a distinct group. He commanded that judges be appointed to judge the judgment that is truly just. ... Since the civil order would not be perfected by this alone, God completed its arrangement through the commandment of the king. ... The king can judge without prior warning according to what he sees the political community requires. Thus the appointment of the king is shared by Israel and the other nations, who require civil order, while the appointment of the judges is especially necessary in Israel.”

paragraphs.text: Connection: The Ran gives the precise institutional distinction presupposed here: Torah courts judge according to the Torah’s judicial requirements, while royal authority can address the community’s practical needs beyond those procedures. This clarifies why Rav Tzadok lists judge, lawgiver, and king as distinct functions before describing their unification in God. The Ran’s civil explanation does not itself supply Rav Tzadok’s mystical identification of the final salvation with Atika.
